planting.note: Plant in spring after frost into sharply drained, gritty soil; avoid winter-wet sites.

directions: Set this gray-woolly Balearic native where summer water is minimal and winter drainage is sharp, since soggy roots in cold weather are its main weakness. Whorls of soft lilac-pink flowers appear along the stems in early summer above the felted, aromatic foliage. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mounded habit tidy and prevent legginess. Give it a sheltered, reflected-heat spot in marginal zones to help it through winter.

planting.note: Plant in spring in lean, fast-draining soil; container culture suits it in colder gardens.

directions: A diminutive Turkish relative of Jerusalem sage, this low mounding shrub carries small scalloped, felted gray-green leaves and short spikes of soft yellow flowers in early summer. Its compact size suits rock gardens, raised beds, and troughs where larger phlomis would overwhelm the space. Keep it on the dry side year-round and resist the urge to feed it, since lean conditions produce the tightest, most floriferous growth. Protect from prolonged freezes and wet winter soil.

common_name: Elsie Heugh Checkerbloom (Fringed Pale Pink Perennial Mallow)

planting.note: Divide and replant in early spring or early fall into fertile, well-drained border soil.

directions: A long-cultivated English border classic, this hybrid sends up slender spikes thick with fringed, satiny pale-pink blooms through mid and late summer. The hollyhock-like flowers open in long succession along upright stems that mix well among other cottage perennials without staking in most sites. Deadhead spent spikes to extend bloom and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor. It resents heavy, waterlogged soil far more than it minds drought.

common_name: Croftway Red Checkerbloom (Deep Rose-Red Perennial Mallow)

planting.note: Divide and replant in early spring or early fall into fertile, well-drained border soil.

directions: One of the deepest-colored sidalcea selections, this cultivar carries saturated rose-red, satiny flowers packed along upright racemes above rounded, deeply cut foliage. It flowers over a long midsummer stretch and pairs well with silver foliage plants that set off the warm flower color. Stake only in exposed, windy borders, since the stems are otherwise self-supporting. Lift and divide every three to four years once the clump's center begins to thin out of bloom.

common_name: Wisley Pink Rock Rose (Silver-Leaved Pink Sun Rose)

planting.note: Plant in spring into lean, sharply drained soil; avoid rich beds that promote rot.

directions: This trailing sub-shrub forms a tight silvery-gray mat smothered each late spring in clear pink, poppy-like blooms that open fresh each morning and shatter by afternoon. Trim the mound back by roughly a third right after flowering to keep growth dense and encourage a possible light rebloom. It thrives on neglect in gritty, low-fertility soil and quickly declines wherever drainage or air circulation is poor. Use it cascading over rock walls or along the front of sunny, dry borders.

common_name: Wisley Primrose Rock Rose (Silver-Leaved Pale Yellow Sun Rose)

planting.note: Plant in spring into lean, sharply drained soil; avoid rich beds that promote rot.

directions: Soft primrose-yellow flowers cover this gray-leaved selection in a dense flush during late spring, the blooms held just above a low, spreading mat of foliage. Like other sun roses it is short-lived on heavy or poorly drained ground but persists for years in a scree bed or dry wall. Shear lightly after the main bloom to tighten the habit and discourage the woody, sprawling growth that develops with age. It combines well with other pastel-flowered rock garden plants that share its taste for lean soil.

common_name: Henfield Brilliant Rock Rose (Flame-Orange Sun Rose)

planting.note: Plant in spring into lean, sharply drained soil; avoid rich beds that promote rot.

directions: This long-favored selection produces vivid flame-orange flowers in generous quantity over dark green foliage, a brighter and warmer effect than the gray-leaved sun rose cultivars. The low, spreading habit makes a dense edging or ground cover on sunny banks and wall tops where soil stays lean and dry. Shear the plant back hard immediately after its main spring flush to prevent the center from opening up and going woody. It tolerates poor, rocky soil far better than any amount of extra watering or feeding.
